The story of AI in a company, in eight steps

From enthusiasm to governed transformation

Not every company starts from the same point. But the steps to bring order are the same, and they come in this order. Follow the path from 01 to 08.

Act I · Understand where you are

  1. It all starts with enthusiasm

    One team tries an assistant. Another automates a report. A vendor gives away a proof of concept. Within a few months there are a dozen AI initiatives and nobody governs them. AI is treated as one more technology.

  2. The board starts to ask

    Does this produce anything? The board and management ask simple questions: whether the company is making progress, whether the cases are profitable, whether risk is under control. Nobody has a single answer. Each answer is a spreadsheet and an opinion.

  3. First, know what you have

    The first job is an inventory: which AI is in use, who is accountable for it and what it affects. With it comes a first reading of maturity. The maturity assessment gives it across seven dimensions and does not reward more technology than governance.

  4. Look outside and decide how much you want

    The sector gallery shows what other companies in your industry do. With the inventory and that reference, the board makes its first decision: how much ambition it wants and how much risk it accepts.

Act II · Govern and grow

  1. Set the portfolio in motion

    The method starts here. Each initiative is recorded and moves through stages. The funnel shows the speed of the transformation: what moves, what gets stuck, what leaves and why.

  2. Figures the board can believe

    The same register feeds the board dashboard: full cost against value, and which share of the value is validated. With those figures, budget and aspirations are discussed seriously.

  3. Govern without slowing down

    Each initiative passes a decision gate before every big spend. The company knows which value it seeks and measures it. It decides what is done and what is not. Stopping in time, with a reason, is a result.

  4. With the house in order, do more

    With the portfolio governed, risk bounded and AI consumption under control, the company decides what else it can do. Now its transformation ambition is real. You do not reach this step without serious governance.

The path is the same. The starting point is not. These eight steps are what SEVEN-G puts in order with documents, templates and tools. Your company may be at step 01 or at step 06. See where you start, check it with example data or choose how much time you have.

The three strategic questions ↓

Three strategic questions

These are not technology questions. They are strategy questions.

AI is not one more technology or one more product. It is an enabler, an accelerator and a transformer of the company. That is why it is treated as a strategic asset. Its decisions do not belong to the technology area alone: they belong to the board of directors, the chief executive and the chief financial officer.

SEVEN-G does not tell you which technology to buy. It helps you answer three management questions, with the data of your own portfolio.

Where to invest

Where AI has most impact in your company, where you are not playing and whether investment follows your strategy.

A heat map of the areas where value is created —customer, product and service, people, operations, data, knowledge, decision— by ambition level, with investment, annual net and the gaps against what management approved.

How to scale

What is stopping you from scaling AI today and where to start.

An executive reading ranks six barriers —unproven value, cases that do not move forward, risk not closed, people who do not adopt it, data and technology, direction— and says what to do first, who and how much value waits behind each one.

See what holds back scaling →See what holds back scaling →

How to prove the value

How much each euro really returns and how much of that figure the board can believe.

Full cost against efficiencies and return, case by case; only what management control has validated adds up, and a gate before each major spend lets you stop in time what does not perform.

See the portfolio and its value →

In the example dashboard, with a fictitious company; with your data, they come from your own initiative register.

Standards —ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act— say what must exist; SEVEN-G is the operating layer that makes it work, initiative by initiative and portfolio by portfolio. It is not an alternative to ISO/IEC 42001 nor a certification: what it covers and what it does not, requirement by requirement.

How it looks in practice · step 06

What the board needs to see, on one screen

The same register feeds a dashboard for the board of directors: costs, return, annual net and how much of that value has been validated by management control.

Swipe the image to see all of it.

  • Annual net of the portfolioCosts, efficiencies and return, with and without cross-cutting platforms.
    ?

    What it shows. Investment, recurring costs, efficiencies and return for each case and the annual net that remains; what is already being obtained versus what could be, and where additional investment would pay off most. Also agility: days from idea to approval and from approval to production, by risk level.

    What the board can decide. Reinforce what contributes most, rethink or retire negative nets with no strategic reason and steer the budget towards the units with the highest return; unblock stalled cases and see whether the bottleneck is approving (governance) or delivering (capacity).

  • Traffic lights nobody can dress upValidated value, regulatory classification and complete controls.
    ?

    How far to trust the figures. How much of the value is validated by management control and how much released capacity has not yet become real savings. The board does not accept unvalidated benefits and asks for a plan to realise that capacity.

    What risk is being taken. Each case's classification under the AI Act (the company's view versus the advisory board's), incidents and breaches with their response times and notifications, controls over agents and assistants, and exposure to AI-enabled attacks. The board requires pending classifications, puts conditions on high-risk cases and sets its risk appetite.

    Whether the information is enough. The data-quality light flags what the company does not yet report, so it can be requested with a deadline.

  • On your phone tooA pocket version to take into the board session.
    ?

    Six views. Portfolio and value, Funnel and life cycle, History and adoption, Risk and compliance, Inventory and Glossary; everything can be filtered by company, unit, status or type of case, and each block shows the conclusion first and the detail on a click.

    From one session to the next. A snapshot of the dashboard is saved at the close of each session: it compares how value, costs and cases evolve and measures whether what was launched is really used. The board reinforces training where use is low, retires what is not used and checks that commitments move forward.

The portfolio, case by case

?

How to read it. Every case, ungrouped. In use: actual annual cost and net and the share of its value validated by management control; in progress: the forecast ("fcst."), which does not add to the net; "no data" is never zero. In the dashboard, the inventory is grouped by company and unit with totals, and each case has a card: what it is, what it is for, its status and its figures.

What the board can decide. Spot duplicates that could be merged, check the balance between cost savings, growth and service, and choose which cases are rolled out across the organisation.

In short. The board moves from receiving reports to asking questions with data: how much does it contribute?, how much is validated?, what has stalled and why?, what risk are we taking?, what has changed since the last session? What it decides is kept in the recommendations register, to follow it up.

CaseUnitStageAmbitionAI ActAnnual costAnnual netValidated

"fcst.": forecast for a case not yet producing; it does not add to the net. "Validated": share of current value validated by management control.

"No data" is never zero. And estimates are never dressed up as validated.

What SEVEN-G is

The whole framework. At no cost. Nothing asked of you.

SEVEN-G is a framework to treat AI transformation as a strategic asset, and not as one more technology or product. It puts investment decisions, governance, risk and value measurement into a single method, from the first idea to operation.

Documents, Word templates and applications that run in the browser, with no server. Use it as is, adapt it or build it into your own methodology —whether you are a company, a consultancy or an independent professional—. The only condition: credit the author and indicate the changes. What you enter into the applications stays in your browser, never on a server, and the whole project can be downloaded and installed on your own host, with one installation per client: where your data is and how to install it.

The risk matrix, as an Excel file

The transformation index

Every company starts from a different place

Where does your company start?

Having no AI at all is not the same as having predictive models in production, an automation centre or a dozen pilots. SEVEN-G tells you where to start according to what you already have, and reads your maturity without confusing having more technology with governing it better.

Your starting point and your journey

What you are looking at: twelve questions that place the company in one of six starting points —from "ground zero" to "at scale"— and a five-stage plan with the 22 implementation milestones: what to do first, who does it and with which template. The demo comes out "at scale"; there is a second example of a company that only uses third-party AI.

How you get there: document 96 orders the milestones of the implementation guide (document 90) according to the starting point; each milestone is attested by a question of the maturity model, so moving forward in the journey means moving up in maturity with evidence.

Open the journey →Read document 96 →

Your maturity, through three lenses

What you are looking at: the company's governance capability (levels 0 to 5 in seven dimensions), the AI it has in use —from rules and RPA to agents that act— and what it affects —tasks, processes, people or the business model—, with alerts when technology runs ahead of governance.

How you get there: the maturity assessment (document 11) gives the first lens; the initiative register gives the other two. Having generative AI or agents does not add maturity: it raises what is required.
